title: United Kingdom | FCA Consumer Duty and Conduct Rules
tagline: Apply the SM&CR Conduct Rules, the Consumer Duty, vulnerable customer guidance and the 2026 misconduct rules in a UK bank.
description:
This quest teaches UK bank staff the conduct standards set by the **Financial Conduct Authority (FCA)** and, for dual-regulated banks, the **Prudential Regulation Authority (PRA)**. It is built around **section 64B of the Financial Services and Markets Act 2000**, which requires banks to notify everyone subject to the Conduct Rules of the rules that apply to them and to take all reasonable steps, including suitable training, so they understand them.

You will cover the six Individual Conduct Rules and four Senior Manager Conduct Rules, the **Consumer Duty** (Principle 12, the cross-cutting rules, the four outcomes and the annual board report, from FG22/5), the FCA's guidance on **customers in vulnerable circumstances (FG21/1)**, complaint handling and the Financial Ombudsman Service, the **non-financial misconduct rules and COCON 4.3 guidance in force from 1 September 2026**, and the **CP26/37 proposal** (a consultation only) to replace the training duty.

It is designed as induction and periodic Conduct Rules training for all Conduct Rules staff, line managers and senior managers. It builds knowledge and does not replace your institution's own policies, procedures or legal advice.
audience: All Conduct Rules staff in UK banks and building societies, at induction and refresher
Line managers who deliver and reinforce Conduct Rules training in their teams
Customer-facing, complaints, collections and product teams working under the Consumer Duty
Senior managers, non-executive directors and the board Consumer Duty champion
Compliance, conduct risk and HR professionals who design and evidence the programme
outcomes: Explain the SM&CR, the Individual and Senior Manager Conduct Rules and the FSMA s.64B training duty
Apply Principle 12, the cross-cutting rules and the four Consumer Duty outcomes to real bank decisions
Recognise and respond to customers in vulnerable circumstances using FG21/1
Describe complaint time limits, the Ombudsman's role and how complaints feed outcome monitoring
Judge when bullying or harassment breaches the Conduct Rules under the 2026 COCON 4.3 guidance
Explain breach reporting, the board's annual Duty review and the status of the CP26/37 proposal

sessions.title: The Conduct Rules and the Duty to Train (FSMA s.64B)
sessions.summary: Meet the Senior Managers and Certification Regime, the six Individual Conduct Rules and the four Senior Manager Conduct Rules, and the statutory duty in FSMA section 64B to notify and train everyone the rules apply to.
objectives: Explain the three parts of the SM&CR and who the Conduct Rules reach in a UK bank
State the six Individual Conduct Rules and the four Senior Manager Conduct Rules in your own words
Describe what FSMA section 64B requires a bank to do, including suitable training
Tell good Conduct Rules training from weak training using the FCA's published indicators

cards.title: Day one: the click-through problem
cards.setting: Conduct Risk office, Northmoor Bank plc head office, Leeds. Monday, 9:05 am.

lines.text: Your desk at Northmoor Bank still smells of new carpet when Grace Adeyemi waves you into the Conduct Risk office.
Welcome aboard. I run conduct risk and compliance here, and you are our new Conduct Rules and Consumer Duty training lead. Your quest starts today.
Grace, it's Rhys in Cardiff on the screen. Honest question: my tellers click through the Conduct Rules e-learning in eight minutes. Is that really training?
That is exactly the right question. The law does not just say 'have a course'. It says we must make sure people understand how the rules apply to them.
And does it cover my cleaners' supervisor and the new non-exec on the board too?
Stage 1 is yours: which rules, which people, and what 'suitable training' really means. By Friday you brief the board champion, Fiona MacLeod.

scenes.heading: Born from a crisis
scenes.narration: After the 2008 crisis and scandals such as LIBOR rigging, a Parliamentary Commission on Banking Standards called for personal accountability. Parliament legislated in 2013, and the regime applied to banks from March 2016.

scenes.heading: Three parts
scenes.narration: The Senior Managers and Certification Regime has three parts: the Senior Managers Regime, the Certification Regime, and the Conduct Rules that set minimum standards of behaviour.

scenes.heading: Almost everyone
scenes.narration: The Conduct Rules reach almost everyone who works in an SM&CR firm. The FCA estimates around 900,000 people across financial services. Ancillary staff are the main exception.

scenes.heading: Sections 64A and 64B
scenes.narration: Section 64A of the Financial Services and Markets Act lets the FCA and PRA make conduct rules. Section 64B tells the firm to notify staff of the rules and take all reasonable steps, including suitable training, so they understand them.

scenes.heading: Senior managers carry more
scenes.narration: Senior managers also follow four extra rules, and under the duty of responsibility they can be held to account if a breach happens in their area and they did not take reasonable steps to stop it.

cards.question: What does FSMA section 64B require Northmoor Bank to do for the people the Conduct Rules apply to?
options: Notify them of the rules that apply and take all reasonable steps, including suitable training, so they understand how the rules apply to them
Send them a copy of COCON once at joining and keep a signed receipt on file
Train only senior managers, because other staff are covered by the bank's own code
Arrange an external exam that every member of staff must pass each year
cards.explanation: Section 64B has two limbs: notify relevant persons of the conduct rules that apply to them, and take all reasonable steps to secure that they understand how those rules apply. Subsection (3) says those steps include suitable training. A receipt for a document, or training only senior managers, would not meet it; no external exam is prescribed.

cards.title: Section 64B in plain English
cards.body:
Section 64B was added to the Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 by the Financial Services (Banking Reform) Act 2013 and has applied to banks since **7 March 2016**.

**Who are 'relevant persons'?**
- people approved by a regulator on the firm's application (senior managers)
- **any employee** of the firm
- **any director**, including non-executives

**What must the firm do?**
1. **Notify** each of them of the conduct rules that apply to them.
2. Take **all reasonable steps** to make sure they **understand how** those rules apply to them.
3. Those steps **include suitable training**.

The word *understand* matters. A rule recited at induction is not enough if a mortgage adviser cannot say what 'treat customers fairly' means in a real sale. 'Suitable' means fitted to the role, which is why the FCA expects role-based examples.

cards.prompt: Sort each feature of a Conduct Rules programme by how the FCA would likely see it.

cards.title: A turn in Cardiff
cards.setting: Northmoor Bank branch, Queen Street, Cardiff. Wednesday, 4:40 pm.

lines.text: We had a near miss. A new adviser kept pressing an older customer to move her savings into a fixed bond because his weekly sales count was low.
She said no twice. He's not a senior manager, so do the Conduct Rules even reach him?
They do. He is a Conduct Rules employee. Rule 4 on treating customers fairly and Rule 6 on good outcomes are both in play, before we even ask about Rule 2.
He did the e-learning. He just never connected it to his targets.
Then our training failed the 'understand how it applies to you' test. Let's decide what to change.

cards.title: Fixing Cardiff's training
cards.situation: Rhys asks you to redesign Conduct Rules training for his 22-person branch after the fixed-bond near miss. Budget is modest and the team works shifts. What do you recommend first?

choices.text: Build short, role-based scenarios (including sales-target pressure), have Rhys lead a team discussion, add them to onboarding, and test understanding afterwards
choices.outcome: This matches the FCA's positive indicators: realistic role scenarios, line manager involvement, onboarding and a measure of effect. It also reaches the real risk, which was target pressure.

choices.text: Ask everyone to repeat the existing e-learning and raise the pass mark to 100%
choices.outcome: Repeating a generic module measures recall, not understanding of how the rules apply to the adviser's own job. The FCA lists simple untailored computer-based training as a negative indicator.

choices.text: Email the branch the full text of COCON with a reminder to read it
choices.outcome: Notification is only the first limb of section 64B. The firm must also take reasonable steps so people understand how the rules apply, and an email of rule text rarely achieves that.

choices.text: Run a one-off workshop with the HR team and record attendance
choices.outcome: Better than an email, but a single HR-led session with no line manager involvement and no refresher matches several of the FCA's weak indicators.

cards.title: Real case: the first Senior Managers Regime case, and the ban that followed
cards.body:
**2018:** The FCA and PRA jointly fined Barclays' then chief executive, Jes Staley, **GBP 642,430** for trying to identify the author of an anonymous whistleblowing letter. The FCA said this was the first case under the Senior Managers Regime and found a breach of **Individual Conduct Rule 2** (due skill, care and diligence), not of integrity.

**2023-2025:** The FCA decided to fine and ban Mr Staley over a letter Barclays sent to the FCA, which he approved, containing misleading statements about his relationship with Jeffrey Epstein. In June 2025 the **Upper Tribunal upheld the ban** and the Final Notice of July 2025 set the fine at about **GBP 1.1m** (the FCA had proposed about GBP 1.8m). The findings: breaches of **Individual Conduct Rule 1** (integrity), **Rule 3** (openness with the regulator) and **Senior Manager Conduct Rule 4** (disclosure).

**Lesson:** the rules bite on individuals, and honesty with the regulator is a rule, not a courtesy.

*Sources: FCA press releases of 11 May 2018 and 26 June 2025; FCA Final Notice, 23 July 2025.*

cards.question: A newly appointed non-executive director at Northmoor says the Conduct Rules training is 'for staff, not the board'. Under section 64B, is the bank still required to notify and train her?
options: No, because non-executives are covered only by company law duties
Yes, because section 64B treats directors as relevant persons the firm must notify and help understand the rules
Only if she also holds a certified function
Only after her first board evaluation, which is when the rules start to apply
cards.explanation: Section 64B(4) lists approved persons, employees and directors as relevant persons. A director, executive or not, must be notified of the rules that apply and helped to understand them through reasonable steps, including suitable training.

cards.title: Make it stick
cards.body:
- **Use the learner's own day.** A teller's Rule 4 case looks nothing like a treasury dealer's Rule 5 case.
- **Talk about grey areas.** Fraud is obvious. Target pressure, cutting corners on checks and staying quiet in a meeting are where people go wrong.
- **Put the line manager in the room.** People copy what their manager does, not what the slide says.
- **Measure understanding, not clicks.** Use short scenario checks before and after, and look at breach and complaint trends.
- **Refresh it.** Build it into onboarding, then revisit when roles, rules or risks change.

cards.title: Stage 1 take-aways
items: The SM&CR has three parts: Senior Managers Regime, Certification Regime and the Conduct Rules.
Six Individual Conduct Rules reach almost all staff; SMFs follow four extra Senior Manager Conduct Rules.
FSMA s.64B: notify relevant persons (approved persons, employees, directors) and take all reasonable steps, including suitable training, so they understand how the rules apply.
The FCA wants role-based, scenario-led training with line managers involved, built into onboarding, refreshed and tested for effect.
Real cases show the rules are enforced against individuals, up to bans for senior managers.

cards.prompt: Think of one decision you made last week. Which Individual Conduct Rule was quietly in play, and how would you explain that to a new colleague in your role?

quiz.question: Which statute requires a UK bank to notify staff of the Conduct Rules that apply to them and to take reasonable steps, including suitable training, so they understand them?
options: Section 64A, which only empowers the regulators to make rules
The Money Laundering Regulations 2017, regulation 24
The Bank of England Act 1998, as amended in 2016
Section 64B of the Financial Services and Markets Act 2000
quiz.explanation: Section 64B places the notification and understanding duty on the firm. Section 64A is the power for the FCA and PRA to make conduct rules, so it is the closest distractor but it does not impose the training duty. Regulation 24 MLR is about AML training.

quiz.question: Which group is generally outside the scope of the Individual Conduct Rules in an SM&CR firm?
options: Non-executive directors who sit on the bank's board of directors
Call centre agents who handle retail customers
Ancillary staff, whom the FCA treats as outside the rules
Junior analysts in the treasury department
quiz.explanation: The FCA says the Conduct Rules apply to almost everyone in an SM&CR firm except ancillary staff. Directors, call centre agents and analysts are all within scope.

quiz.question: Northmoor's mortgage adviser Aled keeps pressing a hesitant customer to take a product because of his monthly target. Which Individual Conduct Rule is most directly engaged?
options: Rule 3: be open and cooperative with the regulators
Rule 5: observe proper standards of market conduct
Senior Manager Conduct Rule 3 on delegating responsibilities to others
Rule 4: pay due regard to customers' interests and treat them fairly
quiz.explanation: Pressuring a customer against her interests is a Rule 4 issue (and Rule 6 for retail customers under the Consumer Duty). Rule 5 concerns market conduct such as trading, and SC3 applies to senior managers only.

quiz.question: What did the FCA add to the Individual Conduct Rules when the Consumer Duty took effect in July 2023?
options: A rule to complete annual Consumer Duty e-learning
A sixth rule to act to deliver good outcomes for retail customers
A rule to report every customer complaint to the FCA
A rule that only applies to the board's Duty champion
quiz.explanation: The sixth Individual Conduct Rule requires Conduct Rules staff to act to deliver good outcomes for retail customers where the firm's activities fall under the Duty. It is a behavioural standard, not a training or reporting rule.

quiz.question: Under the FCA's Conduct Rules guidance, which feature is a NEGATIVE indicator of training quality?
options: Only obvious breach examples such as fraud are used
Line managers help deliver the sessions
Training is built into onboarding and refreshed at regular intervals
The responsible senior manager oversees it
quiz.explanation: The FCA lists obvious-only examples (fraud, missing mandatory training) as a negative indicator because they do not draw out how the rules apply to each role. The other three options are positive indicators.

quiz.question: Which Senior Manager Conduct Rule did the FCA find Jes Staley breached in the case upheld by the Upper Tribunal in 2025?
options: SC1: controlling the business effectively
SC3: delegating responsibilities to an appropriate person
SC4: disclosing information the regulator would expect
SC2: complying with the regulatory system
quiz.explanation: The Final Notice of July 2025 records breaches of Individual Conduct Rules 1 and 3 and Senior Manager Conduct Rule 4, because a letter he approved gave the FCA misleading statements. Control, delegation and compliance (SC1-SC3) were not the basis.

quiz.question: A branch completes Conduct Rules e-learning with 100% completion, but staff cannot explain how Rule 2 applies to their checks. What is the main gap against section 64B?
options: The bank has failed to notify the FCA that the training programme has been completed
Staff have not been helped to understand how the rules apply to them
The bank has failed to use an accredited external training provider
The bank has failed to obtain signatures from each employee
quiz.explanation: Section 64B asks for understanding of how the rules apply, not just completion. There is no duty to notify the FCA of training completion, use accredited providers or collect signatures.

quiz.question: In the 2018 case against Barclays' chief executive over an anonymous whistleblowing letter, which rule did the FCA and PRA find was breached?
options: Individual Conduct Rule 1, acting with integrity
Individual Conduct Rule 2, due skill, care and diligence
Individual Conduct Rule 5, market conduct
Senior Manager Conduct Rule 4, disclosure
quiz.explanation: The 2018 press release says the breach was of Rule 2 and expressly not of Rule 1 (integrity). It was the first case brought under the Senior Managers Regime.

quiz.question: Under the duty of responsibility, when can a senior manager be held accountable for a breach by the bank?
options: When the breach is in their area and they did not take reasonable steps to prevent or stop it
Whenever any breach occurs anywhere in the bank, regardless of what reasonable steps they had taken
Only when they personally profited from the breach
Only when the breach led to a criminal conviction of the bank
quiz.explanation: The FCA explains that an SMF responsible for an area can be held accountable if they did not take reasonable steps to prevent or stop a breach there. It is not strict liability, and it does not need personal gain or a conviction.

quiz.question: Rhys wants proof his new Conduct Rules sessions work. Which evidence best fits the FCA's expectation that effectiveness is assessed?
options: Attendance sheets showing who came to each session
A copy of the slide deck with the rules listed
A note from HR confirming the full training budget was spent on time and on the planned providers
Before-and-after scenario checks plus trends in related complaints and breaches
quiz.explanation: The FCA lists 'effectiveness of Conduct Rules training is assessed' as a positive indicator. Scenario checks and outcome trends measure understanding and behaviour; attendance, slides or spend show only that training happened.

sessions.title: The Consumer Duty: Principle 12, Cross-cutting Rules, Products and Value
sessions.summary: Learn how the FCA's Consumer Duty is built: the Consumer Principle, the three cross-cutting rules and the four outcomes, then apply the products and services and price and value outcomes to real bank decisions.
objectives: Describe the structure of the Consumer Duty: Principle 12, three cross-cutting rules and four outcomes
Explain the reasonableness test and what the Duty does not require
Apply the products and services and price and value outcomes to bank products, including closed products
Describe how the FCA has supervised and investigated the Duty since 2023

cards.title: The forgotten savers
cards.setting: Product and Pricing team, Northmoor Bank, Leeds. Tuesday, 10:30 am.

lines.text: I've pulled the savings book. We have about 40,000 customers still in 'Northmoor Instant Saver 2014'. It closed to new customers years ago.
It pays far less than our current easy-access account. Most of these customers are over 65 and haven't contacted us in years.
And the product is still open to them, so they keep their money there and the bank keeps the margin.
Someone in Finance says the Consumer Duty only covers products we sell today. Is that right?
Let's find out together. Stage 2: what the Duty is made of, and what it asks of products and prices, open or closed.

cards.title: How the Consumer Duty is built

scenes.heading: One principle
scenes.narration: Principle 12, the Consumer Principle, says a firm must act to deliver good outcomes for retail customers. It is a higher standard than the older principle of treating customers fairly.

scenes.heading: Three cross-cutting rules
scenes.narration: Act in good faith. Avoid causing foreseeable harm. Enable and support customers to pursue their financial objectives. These shape everything the firm does.

scenes.heading: Four outcomes
scenes.narration: Detailed rules cover products and services, price and value, consumer understanding, and consumer support.

scenes.heading: In force
scenes.narration: The Duty applied to open products and services from 31 July 2023, and to closed products and services from 31 July 2024.

scenes.heading: A reasonable, prudent firm
scenes.narration: Everything is judged against what a prudent firm doing the same activity, and understanding its customers, could reasonably be expected to do.

items.label: Principle 12
items.detail: Act to deliver good outcomes for retail customers

items.label: Cross-cutting rules

items.detail: Products and services; price and value; understanding; support

cards.title: Cross-cutting rule in action
cards.prompt: Match each cross-cutting rule to the bank behaviour that best shows it.

pairs.right: Telling a customer honestly that a cheaper account would suit her better
Spotting that a new fee will hit customers already in arrears and redesigning it before launch
Making it as easy to move savings to a better rate as it was to open the account

cards.question: Meilin's Finance colleague says the Duty ignores products no longer on sale. What does the FCA say?
options: He is right: closed products are outside the Duty
The Duty applies to closed products and services too, from 31 July 2024
Closed products are covered only if a customer complains
Closed products fall under Principle 6 instead of the Duty
cards.explanation: The FCA's guidance says the Duty applies in full to closed products and services, with the deadline of 31 July 2024. Firms were expected to review them, which is exactly the Instant Saver 2014 problem.

cards.title: Reasonable, not limitless
cards.body:
The Duty is demanding, but it has edges.

- **Reasonableness:** judged against a prudent firm doing the same activity with a proper grasp of its target market's needs.
- **Not a guarantee:** the FCA says the Duty does not mean every customer will always get a good outcome, and it does not make a firm responsible for harms outside its role or control.
- **Higher than before:** where Principle 12 applies, **Principles 6 and 7** (customers' interests; communications) **do not**, because the Duty sets a more exacting standard.
- **Personal too:** Individual Conduct Rule 6 asks every Conduct Rules employee to act to deliver good outcomes where the firm's work is in scope.
- **Proportionate:** smaller firms may evidence it differently, but customers should still get good outcomes.

*Note:* in 2026 the FCA consulted (CP26/23) on clarifying the Duty's scope, including taking business with non-UK customers out of scope. That is a **proposal**; check the final rules before relying on it.

cards.title: The value review
cards.setting: Pricing committee room, Leeds. Thursday, 2:00 pm.

lines.text: The fair value assessment is back. Instant Saver 2014 fails it for customers who have held it more than three years.
Fiona MacLeod, board Consumer Duty champion. What do we know about those customers?
Older, low digital use, many with no contact for years. Moving them would cost us margin.
The margin is not the test. Whether they get fair value is. I want options on my desk by Monday.

cards.title: What to do about the 2014 savers
cards.situation: The fair value assessment shows long-standing Instant Saver 2014 customers get poor value. Many are older and rarely online. What should Northmoor do?

choices.text: Act on the finding: raise the rate or move customers to a fair-value product with clear, tested letters and phone support, record the decision, and monitor results
choices.outcome: This addresses the poor value, supports customers who are less likely to act online, and creates the evidence the board report needs. It reflects the FG22/5 expectation to adapt products and policies when poor outcomes are found.

choices.text: Send one letter telling customers better rates exist and leave the decision to them
choices.outcome: Information helps, but the firm already knows this group is unlikely to act and gets poor value. A single untested letter may not deliver a good outcome.

choices.text: Do nothing, because the product closed before the Duty began
choices.outcome: The Duty applies to closed products from 31 July 2024. Ignoring a known fair value failure would be hard to defend.

choices.text: Close the product and move funds to a non-interest current account
choices.outcome: This avoids the margin issue but likely causes harm and does not support the customers' savings objectives.

cards.title: Real case: the FCA's Duty enforcement pipeline (2026)
cards.body:
In its **Enforcement Watch 2** newsletter (July 2026), the FCA described how it supervises and enforces the Consumer Duty.

- It said it had not expected to use enforcement powers straight away while firms embedded the Duty.
- Three years in, it had **11 investigations** into possible Duty breaches; the **first was opened in August 2024**.
- Most action starts as supervision: the FCA reported **382 interventions** in the last financial year, from a conversation to formal requirements on a firm.
- It also uses skilled person reviews and publishes good and poor practice to show what it expects.

**Lesson for a bank:** enforcement is the tail of the process. Supervisors will ask for your outcome evidence long before any investigation, so the monitoring and board reporting you will meet in Stage 5 are your first line of defence.

*Source: FCA, Enforcement Watch 2, 7 July 2026.*

They apply only to complaints handling
They no longer apply, because Principle 12 sets a higher standard
They are replaced by the Senior Manager Conduct Rules

cards.title: Five questions for any product meeting
cards.body:
1. **Who is this for, and who is it not for?**
2. **Could it foreseeably harm anyone**, especially customers with characteristics of vulnerability?
3. **Is the price reasonable for the total benefits**, including for long-standing customers?
4. **Would we be comfortable showing this decision to the FCA** with our data?
5. **How will we know if it goes wrong**, and who will act?

cards.title: Stage 2 take-aways
items: The Duty = Principle 12 + three cross-cutting rules + four outcomes, judged against a reasonable, prudent firm.
It applied from 31 July 2023 for open products and from 31 July 2024 for closed products.
Products and services: clear target market, needs-based design, monitoring over the whole life of the product.
Price and value: the price must be reasonable compared with the overall benefits, for every customer group.
The FCA supervises the Duty first and enforces where needed; it reported 11 Duty investigations by July 2026.

cards.prompt: Pick one product or service your team touches. Which customer group might be getting a worse outcome than others, and what data would show it?

quiz.question: Which of these is one of the Consumer Duty's three cross-cutting rules?
options: Never charge retail customers an exit fee
Answer every customer call within five minutes
Avoid causing foreseeable harm to retail customers
Offer every customer the best rate in the market
quiz.explanation: The three cross-cutting rules are to act in good faith, avoid causing foreseeable harm, and enable and support customers to pursue their financial objectives. The others are not Duty rules.

quiz.question: From what date did the Consumer Duty apply to closed products and services?
options: 31 July 2024
31 July 2023
1 September 2026
7 March 2016
quiz.explanation: The Duty applied to open products from 31 July 2023 and to closed products and services from 31 July 2024. 1 September 2026 is the non-financial misconduct date; 7 March 2016 is when SM&CR began for banks.

quiz.question: Which list correctly names the four outcomes of the Consumer Duty?
options: Products and services; price and value; complaints handling; financial promotions and advertising
Good faith; foreseeable harm; financial objectives; fair value
Products and services; price and value; consumer understanding; consumer support
Suitability; affordability; transparency; redress
quiz.explanation: The FCA's four outcomes are products and services, price and value, consumer understanding and consumer support. Good faith and foreseeable harm are cross-cutting rules, not outcomes.

quiz.question: Northmoor's fair value review finds a packaged account's monthly fee far outweighs the benefits for customers aged over 70, who cannot claim on its travel insurance. Which outcome is most directly failing?
options: Price and value
Consumer understanding
Consumer support
Market conduct
quiz.explanation: The price paid is not reasonable compared with the benefits for that group, which is the price and value outcome. Understanding and support may also matter, but the core failure is value. Market conduct is a Conduct Rule, not a Duty outcome.

quiz.question: Against what standard does the FCA judge what the Duty requires of a firm?
options: What the largest firm in the market actually does in practice
What a prudent firm in the same activity, knowing its customers, could reasonably do
Whatever outcome each individual customer considers fair
Only what is written into the firm's own terms and conditions agreed with each customer at the outset
quiz.explanation: FG22/5 describes an objective reasonableness test based on a prudent firm carrying on the same activity with the necessary understanding of its target market. It is not set by the biggest firm, each customer's view or the firm's own terms.

quiz.question: Which statement about the Consumer Duty is accurate?
options: It does not guarantee that every individual customer always gets a good outcome
It makes a firm liable for every loss a customer suffers on any product or service it provides
It applies only to products launched after July 2023
It replaces all the FCA's complaints handling rules
quiz.explanation: The FCA says the Duty does not mean every customer will always get a good outcome or impose an open-ended duty beyond the firm's role. It covers closed products and sits alongside DISP.

quiz.question: Meilin finds that customers who bought a loan through a broker get far worse outcomes than branch customers. What does the Duty expect next?
options: Accept the difference, because brokers are separately regulated and responsible for outcomes
Investigate the cause for that distinct group and act to address it
Stop monitoring by channel to keep the board report simple
Wait until complaints from broker customers reach a set level
quiz.explanation: FG22/5 expects firms to monitor whether distinct groups, including by distribution channel, get worse outcomes, and to investigate and address the causes. Waiting for complaints or ignoring channels would not meet that.

quiz.question: According to the FCA's Enforcement Watch 2 (July 2026), when did it open its first investigation into a possible Consumer Duty breach?
options: July 2023
December 2024
August 2024
September 2026
quiz.explanation: Enforcement Watch 2 says the first Duty investigation was opened in August 2024 and that there were 11 by mid-2026.

quiz.question: Which Individual Conduct Rule links each employee personally to the Consumer Duty?
options: Rule 2: act with due skill, care and diligence
Rule 6: act to deliver good outcomes for retail customers
Rule 3: be open and cooperative with regulators
Rule 5: observe proper standards of market conduct
quiz.explanation: The sixth Individual Conduct Rule mirrors Principle 12 at individual level for work within the Duty's scope. Rules 2, 3 and 5 are older rules with different focus.

quiz.question: A new overdraft fee would mainly fall on customers already struggling to repay. Product says it is 'within the terms'. Which cross-cutting rule is the strongest reason to rethink it?
options: Avoid causing foreseeable harm
Act in good faith only in sales conversations
Observe proper standards of market conduct
Provide a written acknowledgement of complaints
quiz.explanation: The harm is predictable before launch, so the cross-cutting rule to avoid causing foreseeable harm applies. Being permitted by the terms does not make it consistent with the Duty.

sessions.title: Consumer Understanding, Consumer Support and Customers in Vulnerable Circumstances
sessions.summary: Apply the consumer understanding and consumer support outcomes, spot sludge versus positive friction, and use the FCA's vulnerable customers guidance (FG21/1) to recognise and respond to vulnerability, with lessons from FCA fines against HSBC and TSB.
objectives: Explain what the consumer understanding and consumer support outcomes expect of bank staff
Tell sludge from positive friction in customer journeys
Use the FCA definition and four drivers of vulnerability, and the TEXAS approach to disclosures
Draw lessons from FCA enforcement on customers in financial difficulty

cards.title: Two calls, one morning
cards.setting: Customer Support Centre, Northmoor Bank, Bradford. Monday, 9:20 am.

lines.text: Imran here, contact centre lead. First call: Mrs Okonjo. Her husband died three weeks ago. She's been asked for the death certificate three times by three different teams.
Second call: a customer trying to close his savings account. Online it takes two minutes to open one. To close it he needs to phone, and our wait time is 55 minutes.
Two very different problems. One is a customer in vulnerable circumstances being worn down. The other may be sludge.
My agents mean well. But they've never been trained on bereavement beyond a script.
Then Stage 3 is your stage, Imran. Understanding, support and vulnerability, done properly.

cards.title: Understanding and support in four scenes

scenes.heading: Understood, not just told
scenes.narration: Consumer understanding means customers can understand what they are told and make timely, informed decisions. Communications should be clear, timely and fitted to the customer, and firms should test that they work.

scenes.heading: Support for the whole journey
scenes.narration: Consumer support means help that meets customers' needs throughout the relationship, so they can use what they bought and pursue their goals.

scenes.heading: As easy to leave as to join
scenes.narration: The FCA expects firms to make it at least as easy to switch, cancel or make a change as it was to buy in the first place.

scenes.heading: Good friction and bad friction
scenes.narration: Some friction protects customers, such as a scam warning before a payment. Friction that deters customers from acting in their own interests, known as sludge, is not consistent with the Duty.

cards.title: Positive friction or sludge?
cards.caption: Based on FG22/5 chapter 9 on the consumer support outcome.

items.label: Example
items.left: Pause and warn before a likely scam payment

items.label: Customer effect
items.left: Time to understand risks and options
items.right: Gives up on switching or complaining

cards.back: Someone who, because of their personal circumstances, is especially susceptible to harm, particularly when a firm does not act with appropriate care.
No. The FCA describes it as a spectrum of risk: any customer can become vulnerable, and circumstances change.
Physical or mental health conditions or illness that affect the ability to carry out day-to-day tasks.
Events such as bereavement, job loss or relationship breakdown.
Low ability to withstand financial or emotional shocks, such as low or erratic income.
Low knowledge of or confidence with money, or low literacy or digital skills.

cards.front: What outcome does the FCA want?
cards.back: Customers in vulnerable circumstances should get outcomes as good as those of other customers.

cards.question: Mrs Okonjo is recently bereaved but financially comfortable and confident with money. Is she a customer in vulnerable circumstances under FG21/1?
options: No, because she has enough money
Possibly yes: bereavement is a life event driver, and vulnerability is a spectrum that can change
Only if she has a diagnosed health condition
Only if she tells the bank she wants to be labelled vulnerable
cards.explanation: FG21/1 lists life events such as bereavement as one of four drivers, and treats vulnerability as a spectrum of risk. Staff should respond to her needs without waiting for a diagnosis or a label.

cards.title: FG21/1: four things firms should do
cards.caption: Summarised from FG21/1. Under the Duty these expectations are now part of delivering good outcomes for all.

items.label: Understand needs
items.detail: Know the target market and the vulnerability in it

items.label: Build staff skills
items.detail: Staff can recognise and respond to vulnerability

items.label: Respond in practice
items.detail: Product design, flexible service and communications

items.label: Monitor and improve
items.detail: Check outcomes for vulnerable customers and act

cards.title: Handling a disclosure: the TEXAS approach
cards.prompt: FG21/1 gives TEXAS as an example of how staff can handle a customer telling them about their circumstances. Put the steps in order.
steps: Thank the customer for telling you
Explain how the information will be used
Seek explicit consent, or check the customer does not object, as the data basis requires
Ask questions to understand the situation and support needs
Signpost to internal support or specialist external help

cards.title: Communications that land
cards.body:
Under the **consumer understanding** outcome a bank should:

- give customers the information they need **at the right time** to make decisions
- write **clearly**, without jargon, and fit it to the customer's level of financial knowledge
- **test** important communications (for example, letters about rate changes) to check people understood them
- watch for signs of misunderstanding: complaints, calls after a mailing, customers not acting when it would help them

Under the **consumer support** outcome it should:

- design support that works for all customers, **including those with characteristics of vulnerability**
- avoid **unreasonable barriers**, including unreasonable extra costs
- monitor the quality of support and fix gaps quickly
- make sure no group of customers is disadvantaged

The Duty does not set call-waiting targets, but the FCA notes that specific rules, such as the complaints rules, still have their own time limits.

cards.title: The power of attorney desk
cards.setting: Northmoor Bank branch, Victoria Street, Belfast, linked by video to Leeds. Wednesday, 11:15 am.

lines.text: Rhys covering Belfast this week. A daughter has come in with a registered power of attorney for her father, who has dementia. Our team says the system can't 'see' attorneys, so she must bring him in.
He can't come in. And the FCA's 2025 review of banks looked at exactly this: bereavement and power of attorney.
It found good practice, but also that all firms had to improve, including on training and outcome testing.
So what do I do right now, with her standing at the counter?

cards.title: The attorney at the counter
cards.situation: A daughter holds a valid, registered power of attorney for her father, who has dementia. The branch system cannot register attorneys, and staff say the father must attend. What should Rhys do?

choices.text: Accept and verify the document under the bank's procedure, escalate to the specialist team to register it, record the customer's needs so she is not asked again, and report the system gap
choices.outcome: This meets the customer's needs now, avoids repeated requests and makes sure the systemic problem is fixed. It reflects FG21/1 and the Duty's support outcome.

choices.text: Tell her the father must attend in person, as staff said
choices.outcome: This puts an unreasonable barrier in front of a customer in vulnerable circumstances and likely causes foreseeable harm.

choices.text: Take a photocopy and promise someone will call within a few weeks
choices.outcome: Better than refusing, but without escalation, a record of needs and a clear timeline, the customer may face delay and repetition.

choices.text: Let her use her father's online banking password to manage things for now
choices.outcome: Sharing credentials creates fraud and security risk and bypasses proper authority. It is not a safe workaround.

cards.title: Real case: HSBC fined over customers in financial difficulty (2024)
cards.body:
In May 2024 the FCA fined **HSBC UK Bank plc, HSBC Bank plc and Marks and Spencer Financial Services plc** about **GBP 6.3m** for how they treated customers in arrears or financial difficulty between June 2017 and October 2018.

- They did not always carry out the right affordability assessments when agreeing arrangements to clear arrears.
- Sometimes they took disproportionate action when people fell behind.
- The FCA linked the failings to weaknesses in **policies, procedures and staff training**, and in spotting unfair treatment.
- HSBC identified the problem itself in 2018, told the FCA, and paid about **GBP 185m in redress to over 1.5 million customers**. It received a 30% settlement discount.

The case pre-dates the Duty and was brought under Principles 3 and 6, but it shows what poor support for struggling customers looks like.

*Source: FCA press release, 23 May 2024.*

cards.title: Real case: TSB fined over collections and recoveries (2024)
cards.body:
In October 2024 the FCA fined **TSB Bank plc** about **GBP 10.9m** for failing to treat customers in arrears fairly between June 2014 and March 2020.

- Its processes created a real risk that **repayment plans were not realistic**.
- Its **training did not fully support staff** to understand customers' circumstances.
- **Incentive schemes** may have pushed staff to prioritise the number of plans agreed over time spent understanding each customer.
- TSB paid about **GBP 99.9m in redress to 232,849 customers**. The full scale emerged from a skilled person review the FCA required in 2020.

The lesson for a bank today: training, incentives and support for vulnerable customers are linked. The Duty now asks firms to make sure incentives are consistent with good outcomes.

*Source: FCA press release, 10 October 2024.*

cards.title: Sludge, positive friction or good support?

items.text: Savings can be opened in-app but closed only by post
A warning and short pause before a payment that matches a known scam pattern
A recorded vulnerability note means a bereaved customer is not asked to repeat her story
Cancellation is buried under five menus labelled 'manage offers'
Asking a customer to confirm she understands the risks before releasing a large pension sum to a new payee
A dedicated bereavement line with staff trained in the process
Complaint forms that require the account number the customer no longer has
Accepting a registered power of attorney at any branch

cards.question: In the TSB case, which factor did the FCA say may have encouraged staff to agree repayment plans without enough attention to customers' circumstances?
options: Incentive schemes that rewarded the number of plans made
A shortage of branches in rural areas
A ban on staff using telephone calls
Customers refusing to give any information
cards.explanation: The FCA said TSB staff were potentially encouraged by incentive schemes to prioritise the number of plans over assessing individual circumstances. Under the Duty, incentives must be consistent with good outcomes.

cards.title: At the front line
cards.body:
- **Listen for drivers**, not labels: health, life events, resilience, capability.
- **Use TEXAS** when someone tells you about their circumstances.
- **Record it once** (with a lawful basis) so they do not repeat painful stories.
- **Remove barriers you control**; escalate the ones you cannot.
- **Spot sludge** in your own journeys and report it. Fixing it is part of the Duty, not a favour.

cards.title: Stage 3 take-aways
items: Consumer understanding: clear, timely, tested communications fitted to the customer.
Consumer support: no unreasonable barriers; leaving or switching should be at least as easy as buying.
Positive friction protects customers; sludge deters them from acting in their own interests.
FG21/1: vulnerability is a spectrum driven by health, life events, resilience and capability; outcomes should be as good as for others.
HSBC and TSB fines show weak training, policies and incentives harm customers in difficulty.

cards.prompt: Walk through one journey your customers use to leave, complain or get help. Where might someone in vulnerable circumstances give up, and what could you change?

quiz.question: How does FG21/1 define a vulnerable customer?
options: Any customer aged over 70 or receiving state benefits of any kind
A customer who has formally registered a disability with the bank at a branch
Any customer whose account balance is below an FCA-set threshold
Someone especially susceptible to harm because of personal circumstances
quiz.explanation: The FCA's definition is circumstance-based, not a fixed category of age, benefits, registration or balance. It stresses susceptibility to harm when firms do not take appropriate care.

quiz.question: Which of these is one of the four drivers of vulnerability in FG21/1?
options: Nationality
Account type
Credit score
Resilience
quiz.explanation: The four drivers are health, life events, resilience and capability. Nationality, account type and credit score are not drivers in the guidance.

quiz.question: A customer can open a savings account in an app in minutes but must phone and wait in a long queue to close it. What does the FCA's Duty guidance say?
options: This is acceptable if the terms disclose it
Closure barriers are fine as long as the savings rate is competitive
It should be at least as easy to switch or leave as to buy
This only matters if the customer complains
quiz.explanation: FG22/5 says firms should make it at least as easy to switch out, leave or make a change as it was to buy. Disclosure in the terms does not cure an unreasonable barrier.

quiz.question: Which is an example of positive friction rather than sludge?
options: Making customers post a letter to cancel a product
Hiding the complaints link under unrelated menus
Requiring repeated proof of death from a bereaved spouse
A pause and warning before a payment that matches a scam pattern
quiz.explanation: Positive friction is designed to prevent harm to the customer, such as a scam warning. The other examples deter or burden customers acting in their own interests, which is sludge.

quiz.question: In the TEXAS approach described in FG21/1, what does the 'S' step involve?
options: Signposting to internal support or specialist external services
Securing a signature from the customer before helping
Suspending the account until a manager reviews it
Sharing the disclosure with all staff in the branch
quiz.explanation: TEXAS ends with signposting the customer to internal support or external specialist help where appropriate. Suspending accounts or sharing widely is not part of it.

quiz.question: In the HSBC fine of May 2024, which causes did the FCA link to the poor treatment of customers in financial difficulty?
options: A cyber attack that disabled the collections system for several months during the period
A government instruction to stop all forbearance during the period
Customers giving false income details on every application
Weak policies, procedures and staff training, and poor checks for unfair treatment
quiz.explanation: The FCA said the failings were caused by deficient policies and procedures, staff training, and inadequate measures to find unfair treatment. The other options are not in the case.

quiz.question: Imran's agents now record a bereaved customer's needs once and share them across teams. Which FCA expectation does this best support?
options: Firms must publish each customer's vulnerability status to the FCA
Firms must avoid recording any information about vulnerability at all, for data protection reasons
Firms must ask customers to repeat details for security on each call
Staff record and reuse relevant information so customers need not repeat it
quiz.explanation: FG21/1 expects staff to know how to record relevant information and how to access it in later interactions, with a lawful basis. Publishing it, refusing to record it or making customers repeat it all miss the point.

quiz.question: Under the consumer understanding outcome, what should Northmoor do before sending a letter announcing a major change to mortgage terms?
options: Make the letter as long as possible so every detail is included
Test the letter to check customers understand it and can act in time
Send it only by email to keep a full audit trail
Rely on the FCA to review the wording before sending
quiz.explanation: The FCA expects firms to test key communications so customers understand them and can make timely decisions. Length, channel or FCA pre-approval are not the test.

quiz.question: What outcome does the FCA want for customers in vulnerable circumstances?
options: Outcomes as good as those for other customers
Outcomes slightly below those for other customers
Priority access to the bank's highest-margin products
Exemption from all fees and charges in every case
quiz.explanation: FG21/1 and the Duty both aim for customers in vulnerable circumstances to get outcomes as good as other customers. That does not mean automatic fee exemptions or product priority.

quiz.question: A branch refuses a registered power of attorney because its system cannot record attorneys, and tells the attorney to bring the customer, who has dementia. What is the best assessment?
options: An unreasonable barrier for a vulnerable customer; escalate and fix the gap
This is positive friction that protects the customer and his money from fraud by others
This is acceptable as long as the refusal is recorded
This is only a problem if the attorney makes a complaint
quiz.explanation: Refusing a valid authority because of a system gap blocks the customer from using his account. The FCA's 2025 review of banks looked at power of attorney, and the Duty expects support without unreasonable barriers.

sessions.title: Non-financial Misconduct: Bullying, Harassment and the Conduct Rules (2026)
sessions.summary: Learn how the FCA's rules and guidance in force from 1 September 2026 treat bullying, harassment and violence towards colleagues as possible breaches of Individual Conduct Rules 1 and 2, how fitness and propriety assessments use non-financial misconduct, and what managers should and should not do.
objectives: Explain what changed on 1 September 2026 and why COCON 4.3 matters to banks
Apply the FCA's seriousness, effect and purpose factors to workplace behaviour
Distinguish Conduct Rules breaches from wider fitness and propriety considerations
Describe what firms should do, and what they do not need to do, under the guidance

cards.title: The group chat
cards.setting: Northmoor Bank, Corporate Banking floor, London. Friday, 5:50 pm.

lines.text: Fiona MacLeod has asked to see you and Grace before the weekend. She has a printout in her hand.
A junior analyst has shared months of messages from a team group chat. Her team leader mocks her accent and her work, and calls her 'the charity hire'. Others join in.
Since 1 September, the FCA's guidance in COCON 4.3 tells us when behaviour like this breaches Conduct Rule 1 or 2.
HR says it's an employment matter, not a regulatory one.
It can be both. Stage 4: when misconduct towards colleagues becomes a Conduct Rules issue, and what our managers must do about it.

scenes.heading: A new rule and new guidance
scenes.narration: From 1 September 2026, a new COCON rule extends the Conduct Rules in non-bank firms to bullying, harassment and violence against colleagues linked to the person's role, and new guidance explains how to judge it.

scenes.heading: Why banks care
scenes.narration: Banks were already in a wider scope, so the new scope rule does not apply to them. But the FCA applies the guidance to banks too, to help decide when such conduct breaches Individual Conduct Rule 1 or 2.

scenes.heading: Integrity or care
scenes.narration: Serious bullying or harassment can show a lack of integrity under Rule 1, or a failure of due skill, care and diligence under Rule 2.

scenes.heading: Fitness and propriety
scenes.narration: Separately, firms can weigh relevant misconduct, wherever it happens, when they assess whether someone is fit and proper, with guidance on private life, social media and unproven allegations.

scenes.heading: Not a licence to snoop
scenes.narration: The FCA is clear that firms do not need to monitor staff's private lives or social media, or re-open past decisions.

cards.title: Is it a Conduct Rules breach? A COCON 4.3 walk-through
cards.caption: A simplified view of COCON 4.3 as published in PS25/23. Always use the firm's HR and legal procedures.

items.label: Start with COCON 3.1
items.detail: The general factors for assessing compliance

items.label: Is it the covered kind of conduct?
items.detail: Bullying, harassment or similar towards a colleague, with a work link

items.label: Is it serious?
items.detail: Pattern, duration, impact, seniority, power over career, history

items.label: Effect and purpose
items.detail: Was dignity violated, as felt and reasonably so, or was that the aim?

items.label: Which rule?
items.detail: Lack of integrity (Rule 1) or of due skill, care and diligence (Rule 2)

items.label: Act and record
items.detail: Discipline, report breaches as required, update fitness assessment

cards.title: Seriousness factors the FCA takes into account

cards.back: Is the conduct repeated, or part of a pattern?
How long did it go on?
Was the effect on the colleague serious and marked, not merely real but minor?
How senior is the person, and is there a seniority gap or power over the other's career?
Has the person been warned or disciplined before, or promised not to do it again?
Is the conduct criminal, or would it justify dismissal?

cards.question: The analyst never made a formal complaint; she only shared the messages informally. Under COCON 4.3, does the lack of a formal complaint make the conduct less serious?
options: Yes, without a formal complaint it cannot be a breach
No. Whether there was a formal complaint is not generally relevant to seriousness, though a complaint can be evidence of effect
Yes, unless the FCA receives a complaint directly
No, because every unkind message is automatically a breach
cards.explanation: The guidance says the existence of a formal complaint is not generally relevant to how serious the conduct is, although a complaint may help show its effect. Not every unkind remark is a breach: seriousness still has to be judged.

cards.title: Effect and purpose: two tests in one
cards.body:
The guidance looks at both **effect** and **purpose**.

**Effect** has two parts that both matter:
- **Subjective:** how did the colleague perceive it? If she did not feel her dignity was violated, the conduct should not be found to have had that effect.
- **Objective:** was it **reasonable** for the conduct to have that effect? If not, it should not be found to have done so.

**Purpose** matters too: conduct whose aim was to violate dignity, or create an intimidating, hostile, degrading, humiliating or offensive environment, can be covered even if it does not actually have that effect (for example, an intimidating message intercepted before it arrives).

**Then the Rule:** conduct of the covered kind breaches **Rule 1** if it shows a lack of integrity, or **Rule 2** if it shows a failure to act with due skill, care and diligence.

A firm's staff handbook breach alone is unlikely to weigh much; a **prior warning** about similar conduct is likely to be significant.

cards.title: COCON or FIT: two lenses on misconduct
cards.caption: The FCA says COCON and FIT operate separately (FCA non-financial misconduct page).

items.label: Focus
items.right: Any relevant misconduct, wherever it occurs

items.label: Question
items.right: Is the person still fit and proper?

items.label: Private life
items.right: Can be relevant if it shows material risk

cards.title: Where does it belong?
cards.prompt: Sort each situation by the main lens a bank would use.
buckets: Not for the bank to pursue

items.text: A team leader repeatedly belittles a junior in team meetings
A manager threatens a colleague at the office party
A trader is convicted of a violent offence outside work
An anonymous rumour that a cashier was rude to a neighbour years ago
A senior manager's public social media posts threaten violence
Routinely scanning every employee's personal social media accounts
A supervisor uses control over bonuses to pressure a colleague

cards.title: The manager's dilemma
cards.setting: Video call between Leeds and London. Monday, 8:30 am.

lines.text: The team leader's manager has asked what to do. He says the team leader 'gets results' and the chat was 'banter'.
Months of messages, a power gap and a junior who says she dreads coming in. That is not banter.
The FCA guidance also covers reasonable steps for managers. What the manager does next matters for him too.

cards.title: What the line manager should do
cards.situation: A line manager learns from the group chat printout that a team leader he supervises has belittled a junior colleague for months. The junior is anxious about retaliation. What should he do?

choices.text: Take it seriously: make sure the junior is safe from retaliation, refer it promptly into the bank's formal process, preserve evidence, and let HR and Compliance assess it against COCON and FIT
choices.outcome: This takes reasonable steps, protects the colleague and lets the bank decide on discipline, breach reporting and fitness. It reflects the FCA's expectation that firms act decisively.

choices.text: Have a quiet word with the team leader and close the matter, given his results
choices.outcome: An informal chat may stop the behaviour for now, but it bypasses the formal process and the regulatory assessment. Results do not excuse serious misconduct.

choices.text: Ask the junior to sort it out directly with the team leader
choices.outcome: This puts the burden on the person with less power and risks retaliation. It is not a reasonable step.

choices.text: Tell the junior to delete the chat so it does not spread
choices.outcome: Destroying evidence harms the investigation and could itself raise integrity concerns.

cards.title: Should, or need not?
cards.prompt: Match each statement to the FCA's position in its non-financial misconduct page.

Firms should review their approach to both
Firms need not re-check whether past conduct breaches were correctly decided
Firms need not monitor employees' private lives or accounts
Firms need not investigate allegations about private life that are trivial or implausible
Firms should make sure they understand how the changes apply to them

cards.title: Real case: speaking up and the Conduct Rules
cards.body:
The FCA's first case under the Senior Managers Regime, in **2018**, concerned a chief executive's reaction to an anonymous letter raising concerns.

- Barclays' then CEO, Jes Staley, tried to identify the author of a June 2016 anonymous letter that included allegations about him.
- The FCA and PRA said he had a conflict of interest and should have kept his distance, leaving the investigation to those responsible for whistleblowing.
- They found a breach of **Individual Conduct Rule 2** (due skill, care and diligence), but not of integrity, and fined him a combined **GBP 642,430**.
- Barclays had to report yearly to the regulators on its whistleblowing handling.

Since 2026, COCON's examples of Rule 1 breaches also include causing a colleague significant detriment for using whistleblowing procedures, and harassment of a colleague.

The link to this stage: a culture where people can raise concerns about colleagues, including bullying or harassment, without fear is a regulatory issue, and how leaders respond is judged against the Conduct Rules.

*Source: FCA press release, 11 May 2018.*

cards.question: Why does the FCA's guidance on harassment in COCON 4.3 apply to banks when the new scope rule (COCON 1.1.7FR) does not?
options: Because banks asked to be included
Because banks are regulated only by the PRA
It does not apply to banks at all
Because the Conduct Rules already reached such conduct at banks, and the guidance helps them judge when it breaches Rule 1 or 2
cards.explanation: PS25/23 explains that the scope of the Conduct Rules at banks was already wider. The FCA applies the relevant part of the new rule to banks as guidance so they can judge when bullying, harassment or violence towards a colleague breaches Rule 1 or 2.

cards.title: For line managers
cards.body:
- **Do not dismiss it as banter.** Ask about pattern, duration, impact and power.
- **Protect the person who spoke up** from retaliation.
- **Use the formal process**; do not investigate alone or promise secrecy you cannot keep.
- **Keep evidence** and notes factual.
- **Know the link to your own rules:** ignoring serious misconduct you manage can raise questions about your own skill, care and diligence.

cards.title: Stage 4 take-aways
items: From 1 September 2026, FCA rules and COCON 4.3 guidance address bullying, harassment and violence towards colleagues.
At banks the guidance helps decide when such conduct breaches Rule 1 (integrity) or Rule 2 (skill, care and diligence).
Seriousness looks at pattern, duration, impact, seniority and power, history and whether it is criminal or dismissal-level.
COCON and FIT are separate: FIT can weigh relevant misconduct wherever it occurs.
Firms need not monitor private lives or re-open past decisions, but must make sure staff and managers understand the changes.

cards.prompt: If a colleague told you tomorrow that a senior person was belittling them, what would your first three actions be, and who in your firm would you go to?

quiz.question: From what date did the FCA's new non-financial misconduct rule and the COCON 4.3 guidance take effect?
options: 31 July 2023
1 September 2026
24 April 2026
22 January 2027
quiz.explanation: PS25/23 says the guidance came into force on 1 September 2026, alongside the new rule at COCON 1.1.7FR. 31 July 2023 is the Consumer Duty date and 22 January 2027 is the CP26/37 closing date.

quiz.question: Under COCON 4.3, serious bullying of a colleague that shows a lack of integrity would breach which rule?
options: Individual Conduct Rule 4
Individual Conduct Rule 5
Individual Conduct Rule 1
Senior Manager Conduct Rule 3
quiz.explanation: The guidance says conduct of this kind breaches Rule 1 where it shows a lack of integrity, or Rule 2 where it shows a failure of due skill, care and diligence. Rules 4 and 5 concern customers and markets.

quiz.question: Which is one of the factors the FCA lists for judging whether misconduct towards a colleague is serious?
options: Whether the colleague works in the same building or on the same floor as the person
Whether the conduct happened on a weekday
Whether the person has a sales target
Whether the person has control or influence over the colleague's career
quiz.explanation: COCON 4.3.8G includes seniority, the seniority gap and whether the person has control or influence over the other's career. Location, weekday and sales targets are not listed factors.

quiz.question: A colleague says a remark was harmless and did not affect her at all. How does the effect test in COCON 4.3 treat this?
options: Her view is irrelevant; only the manager's view counts
The remark is automatically a breach once reported
If she did not perceive the effect, the conduct should not be found to have had it
The effect is presumed unless she denies it in writing
quiz.explanation: The effect test has a subjective part: if the subject does not perceive the effect, it should not be found. There is also an objective part about reasonableness, and purpose can still matter separately.

quiz.question: Which statement about the Conduct Rules (COCON) and the Fit and Proper test (FIT) is correct?
options: They are the same test applied twice by different teams
They operate separately; FIT can weigh relevant misconduct wherever it occurs
FIT applies only to conduct inside the office
COCON now covers all conduct in employees' private lives, whether or not work-related
quiz.explanation: The FCA says COCON and FIT operate separately. The COCON rule focuses on certain work-related misconduct, while FIT can consider relevant misconduct wherever it happens. COCON is not extended into private life.

quiz.question: Which of these does the FCA say firms do NOT need to do under the non-financial misconduct changes?
options: Make sure managers understand how the changes apply
Consider updating staff policies
Monitor employees' private lives or social media accounts
Review their approach to fit and proper assessments
quiz.explanation: The FCA states firms do not need to monitor private lives or social media. It does expect firms to consider updating policies, breach reporting, F&P assessments and references, and to make sure staff and managers understand the changes.

quiz.question: Why does the new scope rule at COCON 1.1.7FR not apply to banks?
options: Banks are exempt from all non-financial misconduct standards
The Conduct Rules at banks already had a wider scope that reaches such conduct
Banks are supervised only by the PRA, not the FCA
Banks asked the FCA for an exemption in their responses to the 2025 consultation
quiz.explanation: PS25/23 explains that the scope of the Conduct Rules at banks was already wider. The new rule aligns non-banks with banks, and the guidance in COCON 4.3 applies to banks too.

quiz.question: A team leader says the bank cannot treat his conduct as serious because he only breached the staff handbook. What does COCON 4.3 say about handbook undertakings?
options: Any breach of the staff handbook automatically counts as a Conduct Rules breach, whatever its seriousness
Handbook breaches can never be relevant to seriousness
Only breaches of the handbook can make conduct serious
A general handbook undertaking matters little, but a prior specific warning is likely to matter
quiz.explanation: The guidance says signing up to the staff handbook generally is unlikely to weigh much, while a previous warning or undertaking not to repeat similar conduct is likely to be significant.

quiz.question: In the 2018 case about an anonymous whistleblowing letter, what did the regulators say the chief executive should have done?
options: Identified the author quickly himself to protect the bank's reputation and the board
Kept his distance and left it to those responsible for whistleblowing
Reported the letter to the police before reading it
Asked the board to vote on whether to investigate
quiz.explanation: The FCA said that, given his conflict, he should have kept his distance and not tried to identify the author, and should have consulted those responsible for whistleblowing.

quiz.question: A manager hears of months of humiliating messages from a team leader to a junior and calls it banter. What is the best response under the 2026 framework?
options: Close it informally because the team leader's results and client feedback are strong
Ask the junior to resolve it directly with the team leader
Wait to see whether the junior files a formal complaint
Refer it to the formal process, protect the junior and have it assessed
quiz.explanation: The pattern, duration and power gap point to possibly serious conduct. The bank needs to assess it properly; informal closure, pushing it back to the junior or waiting for a formal complaint are not reasonable steps.

sessions.title: Complaints, Outcome Monitoring, the Board and What Comes Next
sessions.summary: Bring it together for assessment: complaint handling and the Financial Ombudsman Service, outcome monitoring and the annual Consumer Duty board report, Conduct Rule breach reporting, and the CP26/37 proposal to replace the training duty.
objectives: Describe the main stages and time limits of a bank complaint as the FCA explains them, and the Ombudsman's role
Explain the board's annual Consumer Duty review, the board champion and what good outcome data looks like
Apply the FCA's Conduct Rule breach reporting requirements
Explain the CP26/37 proposal and why the current section 64B duty still applies

cards.title: Board week
cards.setting: Boardroom, Northmoor Bank head office, Leeds. Monday, 8:00 am.

lines.text: The annual Consumer Duty report goes to the board on Thursday. The draft says 'outcomes are good' because complaints fell 12%. I'm not convinced.
Complaints fell because we moved the complaints link behind the login. Customers who are locked out can't find it.
And the FCA has just consulted on dropping the statutory Conduct Rules training duty. The executive committee wants to cancel our new programme.
Then this is the final stage. Complaints, data, the board, breach reporting and the proposals. Get it right and we face the FCA with confidence.

scenes.heading: The customer complains
scenes.narration: Customers can complain to the bank about a product or service. Banks must have a process for resolving complaints fairly, consistently and promptly.

scenes.heading: Acknowledge
scenes.narration: Unless the complaint is resolved within three business days, the bank must let the customer know in writing that it has received it.

scenes.heading: Final response
scenes.narration: In general the bank must give its decision in writing within eight weeks, or explain why it needs more time. Some payment services complaints have shorter limits.

scenes.heading: The Ombudsman
scenes.narration: If the customer is unhappy, or the bank is late, the free and independent Financial Ombudsman Service may help. Customers should normally go to it within six months of the final response.

scenes.heading: Learn from it
scenes.narration: Root-cause analysis turns complaints into fixes, and complaint data feeds the bank's Consumer Duty monitoring.

cards.title: Complaint time limits the FCA explains to consumers
cards.caption: From the FCA's 'How to complain' page. The detailed rules are in the FCA's DISP sourcebook.

items.label: Complaint received
items.detail: The customer tells the bank what went wrong

items.label: Within 3 business days
items.detail: Resolve, or acknowledge in writing

items.label: Within 8 weeks
items.detail: Final written response, or say why more time is needed

items.label: Payment services
items.detail: Normally 15 business days; 35 at most with reasons

items.label: Within 6 months
items.detail: Customer can take it to the Ombudsman

cards.title: Handling a complaint well
cards.prompt: Put these complaint-handling steps in a sensible order.
steps: Log the complaint and acknowledge it in line with the rules
Gather the customer's account and the bank's records
Assess it impartially, including known failings
Decide, put things right and explain in a clear final response
Tell the customer about the right to refer to the Ombudsman
Analyse root causes and feed lessons into training and outcome monitoring

cards.question: A Northmoor customer complains on 2 March. The bank does not resolve it in three business days. What does the FCA say must happen in general?
options: The bank must acknowledge it in writing and, in general, give a written outcome within eight weeks
The bank can wait for the customer to chase before replying
The bank must refer it to the Ombudsman straight away
The bank must give its final answer within three business days
cards.explanation: The FCA's consumer guidance says firms must acknowledge in writing unless they resolve within three business days, and in general give a written outcome within eight weeks or explain why they need more time.

cards.title: Real case: Lloyds Banking Group fined GBP 117m over PPI complaints (2015)
cards.body:
In June 2015 the FCA fined **Lloyds Bank, Bank of Scotland and Black Horse** **GBP 117m**, then its largest ever retail fine, for unfair handling of payment protection insurance complaints between March 2012 and May 2013.

- Lloyds assessed complaints on more than **2.3 million** PPI policies and rejected **37%**.
- Guidance told handlers to presume its sales processes were compliant and robust (the 'Overriding Principle').
- Handlers were **not told about known sales failings**, and some customers' own accounts of the sale were dismissed.
- Some rejected customers were told their complaint had been fully investigated when it had not.

**Lesson:** complaint handling must be impartial and informed. A complaints team that is not told what the bank already knows cannot reach fair outcomes, and complaint data built on unfair handling hides harm from the board.

*Source: FCA press release, 5 June 2015.*
