cards.title: The board report and the Duty champion
cards.body:
The Consumer Duty makes outcomes a **board** matter.

- At least **annually**, the board (or equivalent governing body) should review and approve an assessment of whether the bank is delivering good outcomes consistent with the Duty, and agree any actions.
- The FCA expects a **board-level Duty champion**, ideally an independent non-executive director, who with the Chair and CEO keeps the Duty in all relevant discussions.
- Strategy, governance, leadership and **people policies, including incentives**, should support good outcomes; staff should be trained to deliver them.
- Monitoring should go **beyond complaints data** and look at **distinct groups**, such as customers with characteristics of vulnerability, long-standing customers or particular channels.

In its review of the first board reports from **180 firms**, the FCA praised a clear outcomes focus, good-quality data, analysis of different customer groups and a focus on culture, and wanted better data quality and evidence across distribution chains.

cards.title: Conduct Rule breach reporting
cards.prompt: Match each situation to what the FCA's Conduct Rules page says firms must do.

pairs.left: Non-SMF breach leading to disciplinary action
pairs.right: Report it in the annual REP008 return
Notify the FCA within 7 business days, usually on Form D

pairs.left: SMF breach and the SMF is leaving
Breach not serious enough for disciplinary action
pairs.right: Not reportable as a Conduct Rule breach
Still report, mention the appeal and update later

cards.title: The proposal on the table
cards.setting: Executive committee room, Leeds. Tuesday, 4:00 pm.

lines.text: CP26/37 was published on 22 October 2026. It proposes replacing the Conduct Rules training requirement with a duty to notify staff of the rules and the consequences of breaching them.
So we can cancel the new programme?
No. It's a consultation that closes on 22 January 2027. The statutory duty in section 64B still applies until Parliament and the FCA change it.
And even if it changes, the Duty still expects staff trained to deliver good outcomes. We keep the programme and keep it lean.

cards.title: Today versus the CP26/37 proposal
cards.caption: CP26/37 opened on 22 October 2026 and closes on 22 January 2027; the FCA expects a policy statement in the first half of 2027.

items.label: Training
items.left: Notify and take all reasonable steps, including suitable training (s.64B)
items.right: Notify staff of the rules and the consequences of breach; no training duty

items.label: Non-SMF breach reports
items.right: Only final written warning or dismissal

items.label: Timing
items.right: Up to 14 months for final outcomes

items.label: Certification Regime
items.right: Proposed for removal, with the Directory

cards.title: The board report draft
cards.situation: The draft annual Consumer Duty board report says outcomes are good because complaints fell 12%. Imran knows the fall followed moving the complaints link behind the login. Fiona asks you what to do.

choices.text: Flag the cause of the fall, restore an easy complaints route, add other outcome data (contact patterns, vulnerable customer outcomes, product and value data), and revise the report so the board sees the real picture
choices.outcome: This gives the board accurate evidence and removes a barrier to complaining. The FCA wants monitoring beyond complaints data and a report boards can genuinely challenge.

choices.text: Leave the report as drafted, because complaints did fall
choices.outcome: The fall reflects sludge, not better outcomes. Presenting it as good news would mislead the board and could raise Conduct Rule issues for those involved.

choices.text: Add a footnote about the login change but keep the conclusion
choices.outcome: Disclosure helps, but the conclusion still rests on flawed data and the barrier to complaining remains.

choices.text: Remove complaint data from the report altogether
choices.outcome: Complaints are a valuable source of insight. The fix is to use them properly alongside other data, not to drop them.

cards.back: Owns and oversees Conduct Rules training and can explain how it works and whether it is effective.
An independent non-executive who keeps the Consumer Duty in board discussions with the Chair and CEO.
Reviews and approves the outcomes assessment at least annually and agrees actions.
Bring the rules to life in teams, spot misconduct and act on it.
Assess impartially, know the bank's known failings, find root causes.
Follows the six Individual Conduct Rules, including good outcomes for retail customers.

cards.question: The executive committee wants to cancel Conduct Rules training today because of CP26/37. What is the correct position?
options: Cancel it: the FCA has already removed the training duty
Keep training: CP26/37 is only a proposal and the section 64B duty still applies
Cancel it only for staff below manager grade
Replace it with a single email, which CP26/37 already requires
cards.explanation: CP26/37 is a consultation closing on 22 January 2027, and the training duty sits in FSMA section 64B. Until legislation and final rules change it, the bank must keep notifying and training staff.

cards.title: Your evidence pack for an FCA visit
cards.body:
- **Conduct Rules:** who is in scope, notification records, role-based training content, line manager involvement, effectiveness results, breach log and REP008/Form D submissions.
- **Consumer Duty:** target market and fair value assessments, communication testing, support journey reviews, outcome MI by customer group, the latest board report and actions.
- **Vulnerability:** policies, staff skills training, how needs are recorded, outcome testing.
- **Complaints:** timeliness, root-cause analysis, Ombudsman lessons fed back.
- **Non-financial misconduct:** updated policies, manager guidance, cases and outcomes.

cards.title: Stage 5 take-aways
items: Complaints: acknowledge unless resolved in three business days; final response generally within eight weeks; customers can go to the free Ombudsman, normally within six months.
The board reviews and approves a Consumer Duty outcomes assessment at least annually, supported by a board-level champion.
Good outcome data goes beyond complaints and looks at distinct customer groups.
Conduct Rule breaches: non-SMF disciplinary cases in the annual REP008; SMF cases within 7 business days.
CP26/37 proposes replacing the training duty with notification, but it is only a proposal: section 64B still applies.

cards.prompt: If the FCA asked you tomorrow to show that your team understands the Conduct Rules and delivers good outcomes, what evidence could you put on the table, and what is missing?

quiz.question: According to the FCA's consumer guidance, unless a complaint is resolved within what period must a firm acknowledge it in writing?
options: Five business days
Eight weeks
Three business days
Fifteen calendar days
quiz.explanation: The FCA explains that firms must reply in writing to confirm receipt unless they resolve the complaint within three business days. Eight weeks is the general limit for the final response.

quiz.question: In general, within what period must a bank give a customer the written outcome of a complaint, or explain why it needs more time?
options: Eight weeks
Six months
Thirty business days
Twelve weeks
quiz.explanation: The FCA states that firms must generally give a written outcome within eight weeks. Six months is the usual time for the customer to refer the matter to the Ombudsman after a final response.

quiz.question: A customer received the bank's final response and is unhappy. Within what period should they normally contact the Financial Ombudsman Service?
options: Six months of the final response
Eight weeks of the final response
Three years of the original sale
Thirty days of the final response
quiz.explanation: The FCA's guidance says customers should contact the Ombudsman within six months of the final response or it may not be able to help.

quiz.question: What was the 'Overriding Principle' that featured in the FCA's 2015 fine on Lloyds Banking Group?
options: A rule that every complaint should be upheld to save time and cost
A policy of referring all PPI complaints directly to the Ombudsman
A presumption that its PPI sales processes were compliant and robust
A requirement that customers attend a branch in person to make a PPI complaint
quiz.explanation: Lloyds told handlers to presume its sales processes were robust and did not share known failings, so many complaints were unfairly rejected. The other options were not part of the case.

quiz.question: How often should a bank's board review and approve its assessment of whether it is delivering good outcomes under the Consumer Duty?
options: At least every three years
At least annually
Only when the FCA requests it
Every quarter, by FCA rule
quiz.explanation: FG22/5 says the governing body should review and approve the assessment at least annually and agree any actions required.

quiz.question: Who does the FCA expect, where possible, to act as the board-level Consumer Duty champion?
options: The chief executive officer
The head of complaints
An external consultant
An independent non-executive director
quiz.explanation: FG22/5 says the champion should be an independent NED where possible, working with the Chair and CEO to keep the Duty in all relevant discussions.

quiz.question: Northmoor disciplines a call handler with a formal written warning for a Conduct Rule breach. How should it report this under the current FCA requirements?
options: Include it in the annual REP008 return
Notify the FCA within 7 business days on Form D
No report is needed for non-senior staff
Send a letter to the Financial Ombudsman Service
quiz.explanation: For non-SMF staff, breaches that lead to disciplinary action (including a formal written warning) are reported annually through REP008. The 7-business-day Form D route is for SMFs.

quiz.question: What does CP26/37 propose for Conduct Rules training?
options: Require an annual FCA-approved Conduct Rules exam for every member of staff in scope
Extend the existing training duty to cover customers and suppliers
Replace training with a duty to notify staff of the rules and breach consequences
Remove the Conduct Rules themselves for staff below senior management
quiz.explanation: CP26/37 proposes not replicating the statutory training duty and instead requiring firms to notify staff of the applicable rules and consequences of breaching them. It does not change the rules themselves.

quiz.question: A draft board report claims good outcomes because complaints fell, but the fall followed hiding the complaints link. What is the main problem?
options: Board reports must not mention complaint numbers at all
The fall reflects a new barrier to complaining, not better outcomes
Complaint numbers must be sent to the FCA for checking before the board sees them
Falling complaints always prove the Duty is being met
quiz.explanation: Complaints fell because of sludge. The FCA wants monitoring beyond complaints data and reports that let boards challenge the evidence; using this fall as proof would mislead the board.

quiz.question: Under the CP26/37 proposals, which Conduct Rule breach reporting requirement would stay the same?
options: The threshold for non-SMF reporting
The timing for non-SMF final outcomes
Reporting for senior managers (SMFs)
The Certification Regime and the Directory
quiz.explanation: CP26/37 proposes raising the non-SMF reporting threshold, allowing up to 14 months for final outcomes and removing the Certification Regime and Directory, but keeping existing SMF reporting requirements.

bank.question: Northmoor appoints a contractor who works under the bank's day-to-day direction and control to handle customer calls. Under FSMA section 64A, which statement best describes her position?
options: She is outside the Conduct Rules because she has no employment contract directly with the bank itself
She is covered only if the PRA has approved her as a senior manager in advance
She can count as an employee, as she personally serves under the bank's direction and control
She is covered only after completing twelve months of continuous service
bank.explanation: Section 64A treats a person who personally provides services and is subject to the firm's supervision, direction or control as an employee for these purposes. Approval and length of service are not the test.

bank.question: Which pair correctly matches FSMA sections to their role in the Conduct Rules regime?
options: Section 64A makes firms notify and train staff; section 64B sets the financial penalties for individuals who breach them
Section 64A covers senior managers only; section 64B covers all other employees
Section 64A sets the Consumer Duty; section 64B sets the complaint time limits
Section 64A lets the FCA and PRA make conduct rules; section 64B makes firms notify and train relevant persons
bank.explanation: Section 64A is the rule-making power; section 64B places the notification and understanding duty, including suitable training, on authorised persons.

bank.question: A Northmoor senior manager delegates oversight of a collections process to a deputy with no relevant experience and never checks progress. Which Senior Manager Conduct Rule is most at risk?
options: SC3, on delegating to an appropriate person and overseeing it effectively
SC4, on disclosing information the FCA would expect
Individual Conduct Rule 5, on market conduct
Individual Conduct Rule 3, on being open and cooperative with the regulators
bank.explanation: SC3 requires delegation to an appropriate person and effective oversight. The facts show both an unsuitable delegate and no oversight. SC4 and Rules 3 and 5 concern disclosure and markets.

bank.question: The responsible senior manager at Northmoor cannot explain how Conduct Rules training is designed or whether it works, saying 'HR handles it'. How would the FCA's published indicators view this?
options: As good practice, because delegating training to specialists shows effective governance
As irrelevant, because the FCA only looks at completion rates for training
As a negative indicator: the SMF should show involvement in and oversight of training
As acceptable, provided HR has a written training policy approved by the board
bank.explanation: The FCA lists 'relevant SMF has limited knowledge of training approach and/or has delegated with limited oversight' as a negative indicator. Delegation is fine; lack of oversight is not.

bank.question: A treasury dealer at Northmoor shares a client's large pending order with a friend at another firm. Which Individual Conduct Rule is most specifically engaged, beyond integrity?
options: Rule 5: observe proper standards of market conduct
Rule 6: deliver good outcomes for retail customers
Rule 3: be open and cooperative with regulators
SC2: ensure your area complies with the rules
bank.explanation: Leaking order information is a market conduct issue under Rule 5 (as well as integrity under Rule 1). Rule 6 relates to retail customers; SC2 applies only to senior managers.

bank.question: Why did the FCA say the Jes Staley case, upheld by the Upper Tribunal in 2025, involved a breach of Individual Conduct Rule 3?
options: Because he failed to complete Conduct Rules training before becoming chief executive of the group
Because a letter he approved gave the FCA misleading statements about his links with Epstein
Because he tried to identify an anonymous whistleblower in 2016
Because Barclays mis-sold products to retail customers during his tenure
bank.explanation: The 2025 findings were about the misleading letter to the FCA: Rule 1 (integrity), Rule 3 (openness with the regulator) and SC4. The whistleblower matter was the separate 2018 case under Rule 2.

bank.question: Which design best meets both limbs of section 64B for a new cohort of 30 mortgage advisers?
options: Give them the full COCON text and ask each adviser to sign that they have read and understood it before starting work
Tell them which rules apply, then run role-based scenarios, test understanding and reinforce in team meetings
Enrol them in the bank-wide generic module and track completion to 100% within a month
Wait until their first annual appraisal, then cover the rules in a single classroom session
bank.explanation: Section 64B needs notification plus reasonable steps so people understand how the rules apply to them, including suitable training. Role-based scenarios with testing and reinforcement do both; the others cover notification or completion only.

bank.question: An adviser says Individual Conduct Rule 6 does not apply to him because he serves only large corporate clients. What is the best response?
options: Rule 6 applies to every activity of a bank whatever the client type, so his argument fails and it binds all his work
Rule 6 replaced Rule 4, so he now has no customer-related conduct rule at all
Rule 6 applies only to senior managers, so non-senior staff can ignore it
Rule 6 covers work within the Consumer Duty, aimed at retail customers, but Rules 1 to 5 still apply to him
bank.explanation: The FCA says the sixth rule applies where the firm's activities are covered by the Duty, which concerns retail customers. The other five Individual Conduct Rules, including Rule 4, still apply to him.

bank.question: Which piece of history explains why the SM&CR focused on personal accountability?
options: The Consumer Duty review of 2023 found individuals were not being held to account
A European Union directive required all member states to adopt it in 2016
The Financial Ombudsman Service asked Parliament for powers to fine individuals
A Parliamentary Commission on Banking Standards, set up after the 2008 crisis and conduct scandals such as LIBOR, recommended it
bank.explanation: The FCA explains that the PCBS, set up after the 2008 crisis and failings like LIBOR manipulation, recommended a new accountability framework, which Parliament legislated for in 2013.

bank.question: Northmoor's legacy credit card, closed to new applicants in 2019, carries fees far higher than its current card for the same features. What does the Duty require?
options: Review the closed product against the Duty, including fair value, and act on any poor outcomes found
Nothing, because the Duty applies only to products still on sale to new customers on or after 31 July 2023
Only a letter telling customers they may apply for the current card
Wait until customers complain, then review the product case by case
bank.explanation: The Duty applies in full to closed products and services from 31 July 2024, and FG22/5 expects firms to review them. A letter alone or waiting for complaints may not deliver fair value.

bank.question: Which statement best describes the relationship between the Consumer Duty's cross-cutting rules and the four outcomes?
options: The four outcomes replace the cross-cutting rules once a product is launched
The cross-cutting rules apply only to sales, and the outcomes apply only after sale
The cross-cutting rules apply across all conduct and help interpret the outcomes; meeting the four outcomes alone is not the whole of the Duty
The outcomes are guidance only, while the cross-cutting rules are the only binding rules
bank.explanation: FG22/5 says the cross-cutting rules apply across all areas of firm conduct, inform the outcomes, and cover areas the outcomes do not, so complying with the outcomes is not exhaustive of the Principle.

bank.question: Northmoor uses risk-based pricing so some customer groups pay more for loans. How does FG22/5 say this should be handled?
options: Different prices for different groups always breach the Duty
Differences may be compatible with the Duty, but the bank must be able to evidence why they are
Risk-based pricing is outside the Duty altogether because it is a credit risk decision for the lender
The bank must charge every group the same rate to avoid discrimination
bank.explanation: FG22/5 says that where a firm considers different outcomes for distinct groups compatible with the Duty, for example under risk-based pricing, it must be able to evidence this.

bank.question: Which statement about Principle 12 and the older Principles is correct for Northmoor's retail business?
options: Principles 6 and 7 apply in addition and override Principle 12
Principle 12 applies only to firms without a retail business
Where Principle 12 applies, Principles 6 and 7 do not
Principle 12 applies only to products that have a complaint record
bank.explanation: FG22/5 explains that Principles 6 and 7 do not apply where Principle 12 applies, because Principle 12 is a higher and more exacting standard.

bank.question: During a product launch, Sales argues that a new savings bond is fine because 'the Duty is about outcomes, so we will fix problems if they arise'. Which part of the Duty does this most clearly misunderstand?
options: The rule that all savings products must offer the best rate available in the market
The ban on launching products before the FCA approves them
The rule that only the board can approve new products
The expectation to avoid foreseeable harm, including at the design stage
bank.explanation: The cross-cutting rule to avoid foreseeable harm requires firms to identify and mitigate risks before they materialise, including in design. There is no best-rate rule, FCA pre-approval or board-only approval rule.

bank.question: Which description of 'fair value' is consistent with the FCA's explanation of the price and value outcome?
options: The product is priced at or below the average price charged by competitors
The product's price has been disclosed clearly before the customer signs
The price a customer pays is reasonable compared with the overall benefits, taking account of all costs including non-financial ones
The firm earns no more than a set profit margin fixed by the FCA
bank.explanation: The FCA describes fair value as the price being reasonable compared with the overall benefits, looking at fees, charges, limitations and non-financial costs. Disclosure or competitor averages are not the test, and there is no FCA margin cap.

bank.question: What did the FCA's July 2026 Enforcement Watch say about how it has used its powers on the Consumer Duty?
options: It had fined every large bank for Duty breaches by the end of 2025
It had decided not to investigate any Duty breaches until 2028
It had 11 Duty investigations, the first opened in August 2024
It had transferred Duty enforcement to the Financial Ombudsman Service
bank.explanation: Enforcement Watch 2 reported 11 investigations into potential Duty breaches, the first opened in August 2024, alongside 382 supervisory interventions in the last financial year.

bank.question: In 2026 the FCA consulted in CP26/23 on the Duty's scope. How should a bank's training describe this?
options: As final rules that have already removed all business and wholesale customers from the Duty
As a proposal, including removing business with non-UK customers from scope
As a decision to abolish the four outcomes in 2027
As a change that removed closed products from the Duty
bank.explanation: CP26/23 consulted on targeted changes, including removing business with non-UK customers from scope; the FCA expected a policy statement in Q1 2027. Until then it is a proposal.

bank.question: Northmoor's monitoring shows long-standing mortgage customers on reversion rates get worse outcomes than new customers. Which FG22/5 point best guides the next step?
options: Long-standing customers are excluded from monitoring because they chose not to switch
Only groups with protected characteristics under the Equality Act must be monitored
Differences are acceptable if disclosed in the original mortgage offer
Firms should spot distinct groups getting worse outcomes, investigate the cause and act, applying the same analytical effort used for sales
bank.explanation: FG22/5 names long-standing customers as a group firms could consider, says monitoring is not limited to vulnerability or protected characteristics, and asks whether firms segment outcomes as carefully as they target sales.

bank.question: Northmoor's app lets customers switch to a fixed-rate saver in two taps, but switching back needs a branch visit. Under FG22/5, how should this be assessed?
options: As positive friction, because a branch visit helps protect customers from scams
As acceptable, because the Duty sets no rules on customer journeys
As a breach only if a customer formally complains about it
As a likely unreasonable barrier: leaving should be as easy as buying
bank.explanation: FG22/5 expects firms to make it at least as easy to switch out, leave or change as to buy. A one-sided barrier that protects revenue rather than the customer is sludge.

bank.question: A customer says she has recently lost her job and is struggling to read long letters because of anxiety. Which FG21/1 drivers are present?
options: Capability only, because she struggles with reading
Life events and health, with possible effects on resilience
None, because she has not asked for help
Health only, because anxiety is a medical issue
bank.explanation: Job loss is a life event and anxiety affecting day-to-day tasks is a health driver; losing income may also reduce resilience. Vulnerability does not depend on the customer asking for help.

bank.question: Which statement about how FG21/1 and the Consumer Duty fit together is correct, according to the FCA's 2025 retail banks review?
options: FG21/1 was withdrawn when the Duty came into force in July 2023
The Duty builds on FG21/1, which remains relevant guidance
FG21/1 now applies only to insurers, not to banks or building societies
The Duty sets lower expectations for vulnerable customers than FG21/1
bank.explanation: The FCA's 2025 review says the Duty builds on the Vulnerability Guidance, which remains relevant, with the aim that customers in vulnerable circumstances get outcomes as good as others.

bank.question: An agent records that a customer has a hearing impairment and prefers webchat. Under the TEXAS approach in FG21/1, what should come straight after thanking the customer?
options: Explaining how the information will be used
Asking for a medical certificate
Signposting to an external charity
Closing the call and sending a letter
bank.explanation: TEXAS runs Thank, Explain how the information will be used, consent or checks, Ask questions, then Signpost. Signposting comes last; medical evidence is not a TEXAS step.

bank.question: What lesson about incentives does the FCA's 2024 TSB fine offer a bank designing its collections scorecard?
options: Rewarding the number of plans agreed can crowd out understanding of customers
Collections staff should never receive any form of performance pay or bonus linked to results
Incentives are only a problem if they are linked to product sales
Incentive design is a matter for HR and outside FCA interest
bank.explanation: The FCA said TSB's incentive schemes potentially encouraged staff to prioritise the number of plans over assessing circumstances. Under the Duty, incentives must be consistent with good outcomes, not banned altogether.

bank.question: In the HSBC fine of 2024, why did the FCA give credit despite the failings?
options: HSBC identified the issue, told the FCA and paid large-scale redress
HSBC showed that none of its customers had suffered any harm
HSBC proved its staff training had been fully adequate throughout the whole period
HSBC transferred all affected accounts to another lender
bank.explanation: The FCA said HSBC deserved credit for identifying the issue and putting it right, including redress of about GBP 185m to over 1.5 million customers; it also had a 30% settlement discount.

bank.question: Northmoor plans to send a 14-page letter about changes to overdraft charges. Customer research shows many recipients have low financial confidence. What does the consumer understanding outcome most require?
options: Make it clear and tailored, test it, and check people understood
Send it as planned, because full disclosure of every change is what the outcome requires
Add a glossary at the end and send it by post only
Send it only to customers who have complained before
bank.explanation: The outcome expects clear, timely communication fitted to customers' financial literacy, and testing so customers understand. Full disclosure alone does not show understanding.

bank.question: A contact centre leader proposes removing all checks before large payments to new payees because customers find them annoying. What is the best Duty-based reply?
options: Remove them, because any friction is sludge under the Duty
Keep them only for customers aged over 75
Keep well-designed checks that protect customers from scams, because positive friction to prevent harm is expected
Remove them if customers sign a waiver in the app
bank.explanation: FG22/5 distinguishes positive friction designed to prevent harm, which is appropriate, from sludge. Blanket removal or age-based rules would not deliver good outcomes for everyone.

bank.question: A manager's hostile, intimidating email to a colleague is stopped by the bank's filters before it is delivered. Can it still breach the Conduct Rules under COCON 4.3?
options: No, because the colleague never saw it, so there was no effect
Yes: conduct aimed at that effect can breach even if the effect never occurs
No, because only conduct that the intended victim actually reports can ever be a breach
Yes, but only if the manager is a senior manager under the SMR
bank.explanation: COCON 4.3.15G says purpose is relevant as well as effect, and gives the example of a hostile, intimidatory message intercepted before receipt.

bank.question: A colleague says a team leader's comment made her feel humiliated, but the comment was a reasonable, polite request to fix an error. Under COCON 4.3's effect test, what follows?
options: If it was not reasonable for the comment to have that effect, it should not be found to have had it
Her perception alone decides the matter, so it is a breach
The comment is a breach because she reported it in writing
The test is decided by the team leader's intention only
bank.explanation: The effect test has subjective and objective parts. Even if she felt humiliated, if it was not reasonable for the conduct to have that effect, it should not be found to have done so.

bank.question: Which factor would MOST increase the seriousness of misconduct under COCON 4.3?
options: The colleague did not file a formal written complaint
The conduct happened only once and had a minor effect
The person had signed the staff handbook like everyone else
The person was warned before about similar behaviour and promised not to repeat it
bank.explanation: A previous warning or specific undertaking not to repeat similar conduct is likely to be significant. A general handbook signature is unlikely to weigh much, and a lack of formal complaint is not generally relevant.

bank.question: An anonymous message alleges that a cashier was rude to a neighbour years ago. Nothing else supports it. What does the FCA say about such private-life allegations?
options: Firms must investigate every allegation about any employee's private life, however it arrives
Firms must report the allegation to the FCA within seven business days
Firms need not investigate trivial, implausible or irrelevant private-life allegations
Firms must suspend the employee until the allegation is disproved
bank.explanation: The FCA's non-financial misconduct page says firms do not need to investigate trivial, implausible or irrelevant private-life allegations or monitor private lives.

bank.question: Under the 2026 changes, which example of conduct does COCON now give as a breach of Individual Conduct Rule 1?
options: Missing a mandatory training deadline by a few days for a good reason
Subjecting a colleague to significant detriment for using the firm's whistleblowing procedures
Disagreeing strongly with a manager in a team meeting
Making an honest error in a customer's address
bank.explanation: The 2026 instrument added, as a Rule 1 example, subjecting a fellow worker to significant detriment for whistleblowing or for complying with Rule 3 or SC4, alongside harassment of a colleague.

bank.question: Which steps does the FCA say firms should have considered in response to the non-financial misconduct changes?
options: Updating staff policies, breach reporting, fit and proper assessments and regulatory references
Re-running every fit and proper assessment made in the last five years for all certified staff and senior managers
Monitoring all employees' personal social media accounts
Re-opening all past decisions on conduct rule breaches
bank.explanation: The FCA lists staff policies, breach reporting, F&P assessments and regulatory references, and says firms do not need to revise past assessments, re-check past breach decisions or monitor private social media.

bank.question: A senior trader posts threats of violence on his public social media in his private life. Which lens is most directly relevant for Northmoor?
options: Individual Conduct Rule 5, because he is a trader
Nothing, because conduct in private life is always outside the FCA's interest and the bank's
His fitness and propriety, because FIT can weigh relevant misconduct wherever it occurs
The Consumer Duty, because posts are public communications
bank.explanation: The FCA explains that FIT allows firms to consider relevant misconduct wherever it occurs, with guidance on social media; threats of violence are an example PS25/23 treats as relevant.

bank.question: A line manager learns of repeated harassment in his team but takes no action because 'HR deals with that'. Beyond the harasser, whose conduct may now be in question?
options: Nobody else's, because only the harasser can breach the rules
The line manager's own, for failing to take reasonable steps
The HR director's alone, because harassment is an HR matter
The victim's, for not using the formal grievance process
bank.explanation: PS25/23 includes guidance on reasonable steps for managers to protect staff from non-financial misconduct. Ignoring known serious misconduct can raise questions about a manager's own skill, care and diligence.

bank.question: A payment services customer complains about a failed transfer. According to the FCA, what is the normal time for the bank's response and the outside limit with reasons?
options: 8 weeks normally, and 6 months at most
3 business days normally, and 15 business days at most
30 calendar days normally, and 60 days at most
15 business days normally, and 35 business days at most if it explains the delay
bank.explanation: The FCA says payment service providers must normally respond to certain complaints within 15 business days and, if they cannot, give a final response within 35 business days with reasons for the delay.

bank.question: A customer accepts the Financial Ombudsman Service's decision in her favour. What is the position for the bank?
options: The bank may choose whether to comply
The bank can appeal to the FCA to overturn it
The bank need comply only if the award is small
The bank must comply with the decision
bank.explanation: The FCA explains that if the Ombudsman decides in the customer's favour and the customer accepts, the firm must comply.

bank.question: Which lesson from the 2015 Lloyds PPI complaints fine is most relevant to Northmoor's complaint handlers today?
options: Handlers must assess impartially and know the bank's known failings
Handlers should presume the bank's processes are robust unless the customer proves otherwise
Handlers should reject complaints quickly to keep within the time limits
Handlers should rely on the bank's records rather than the customer's account
bank.explanation: Lloyds told handlers to presume sales were robust and did not share known failings, so many complaints were unfairly rejected. The distractors repeat the very failings the FCA criticised.

bank.question: Which feature did the FCA's review of the first Consumer Duty board reports from 180 firms identify as an area for improvement?
options: Reports that had dedicated sections on each of the four outcomes
Data quality that was not good enough to justify conclusions or give the board assurance
Reports that analysed outcomes for groups of customers with characteristics of vulnerability
Reports that discussed the firm's culture and commitment to the Duty
bank.explanation: The FCA praised outcome-by-outcome structure, analysis of customer groups and a culture focus, and listed better data quality as an area for improvement.

bank.question: A senior manager at Northmoor receives a final written warning for a Conduct Rule breach and is staying in role. What must the bank do under current FCA requirements?
options: Include it in the annual REP008 return with other staff
Notify the FCA only if the senior manager appeals
Notify the Financial Ombudsman Service within 8 weeks
Notify the FCA within 7 business days of concluding the disciplinary action, using Form D
bank.explanation: For SMFs, the FCA requires notification within 7 business days of concluding disciplinary action, using Form D (or Form C if leaving). REP008 is for non-SMF staff.

bank.question: Under CP26/37, which non-SMF disciplinary outcomes would still need to be reported to the FCA as Conduct Rule breaches?
options: Any formal written warning, suspension or pay reduction
Only dismissals followed by a criminal conviction
Final written warnings and dismissals
None, because non-SMF reporting would end entirely
bank.explanation: CP26/37 proposes raising the non-SMF threshold so only disciplinary action resulting in a final written warning or dismissal is reported. Today's broader definition includes any formal written warning, suspension, dismissal or remuneration reduction.

bank.question: Fiona asks why the bank should keep investing in Conduct Rules training while CP26/37 is open. Which answer is most accurate?
options: Training is no longer needed because the FCA has said the Conduct Rules are being removed
Section 64B still applies until changed, and the Duty expects trained staff
Training must continue only because CP26/37 makes it compulsory from 2027
Training is needed only for staff who will remain certified after 2027
bank.explanation: CP26/37 is a proposal; the section 64B duty remains until legislation and final rules change it. FG22/5 also expects people to be trained to deliver good outcomes. The Conduct Rules themselves are not being removed.

bank.question: Northmoor's draft board report uses complaint numbers as its only outcome evidence. Which FG22/5 point most directly challenges this?
options: Complaints data must never appear in a Consumer Duty board report
Complaints data is useful, but MI should go beyond it
Board reports must be approved by the FCA before the board sees them
Complaint numbers are the FCA's required single measure of good outcomes
bank.explanation: FG22/5 says complaints data can be valuable but firms should develop MI beyond it. There is no ban on using complaints, no FCA pre-approval and no single required measure.
